grammar.title: Gramática
grammar.rule: el libro: lo busca; la carta: la guarda; los nombres: los lee; las sillas: las lleva.

grammar.note_en:
A direct object is the person or thing directly affected by a verb such as seek, find, keep or bring. In Rosa busca el libro, “Rosa looks for the book”, el libro is the direct object. When that object is already clear, Spanish can replace its full name with a short object pronoun before the finite verb: Lo busca means “She looks for it”. A finite verb is a verb marked for a subject and tense, such as busca or trae. This chapter keeps the pronoun separate and before that finite present verb: lo busca, la guarda, los lee, las lleva. 

Choose lo for a masculine singular object, la for a feminine singular object, los for masculine plural and las for feminine plural. Match the object, not the person acting: Rosa busca el libro becomes Lo busca, because libro is masculine singular even though Rosa is a woman. Elena tiene una carta; la guarda means “Elena has a letter; she puts it away”, with feminine la referring to carta. Ana escribe dos nombres; los lee means “Ana writes two names; she reads them”. Luis mira las dos sillas. Las lleva a una esquina del patio means “Luis looks at the two chairs. He carries them to a corner of the courtyard”. The reference table repeats those noun-to-pronoun relationships. A pronoun needs a clear antecedent: the earlier word or phrase that tells you what it refers to. When the story changes from book to paper, it names the new object before using lo again. A mixed group such as la lista y el papel uses masculine plural los: Ana no los deja en la mesa means “Ana does not leave them on the table”.

Do not confuse a pronoun with an article that looks the same. In la carta, la stands before a noun and means “the”. In la guarda, la stands before a verb and replaces “the letter”. Likewise los nombres contains an article; los lee contains an object pronoun. No stays before the pronoun: No lo encuentra means “She does not find it”; No los deja en la mesa means “She does not leave them on the table”. These object pronouns are not the le/les forms in gustar from chapter10. This course uses standard Mexican object agreement, without replacing a masculine thing’s lo with le.

Relative que joins a noun to a clause that identifies or describes it. A clause is a group with a verb. El libro que lee Rosa means “the book that Rosa reads”; the known book is the antecedent, and que connects it to lee Rosa. El libro que tiene letras grandes means “the book that has large letters”. In the first example Rosa is the subject of lee and the book is what she reads; in the second the book itself is the subject of tiene. Que does not change for masculine/feminine or singular/plural: el papel que recoge Ana, “the paper that Ana picks up”; las personas que llegan al patio, “the people who arrive in the courtyard”. Spanish keeps this connector in the examples even where English can omit “that”. Do not insert another object pronoun inside an object relative: el libro que lee Rosa already expresses the book’s role. Separate main clauses can use an object pronoun when the referent is clear.

The chapter title Lo que falta means “what is missing”, pointing here to the known borrowed book. The reading examples connect que to a clear noun already in the scene. Los libros que vende la madre means “the books the mother sells”; these have a price because they are her private books for sale. El libro que busca Rosa means “the book Rosa is looking for”; it is a library loan. Those relative clauses distinguish real candidates in the search rather than merely adding descriptions.

Encontrar means find; buscar, already known, means look for. Finding is a successful result, so no lo encuentra says the search has not located the object. The shown present forms are encuentro, “I find”, encuentra, “he/she/usted finds”, and encuentran, “they/ustedes find”; the stressed stem has ue in these forms. Perder means lose: No quiero perder el libro means “I do not want to lose the book”. Guardar is keep or put away safely; recoger pick up or collect; entregar hand over or deliver; traer bring toward the relevant person/place. The story shows recoger both for the floor paper and the proposed collection of family books. Traigo, “I bring”, is the shown irregular first-person form of traer; trae is “he/she brings”. Regular -ar/-er plural patterns remain those previously taught. Practise the present forms shown in the story.

Comprar is buy and vender sell. Ana gives dinero, money, and receives a personal book with a precio, price. That is a purchase, unlike borrowing and returning the library book. The numbers on the price cards identify the two books in the story. A lista is a list. Vacío/vacía mean empty, agreeing with the noun: the white silla is vacía, the armario vacío. Completo/completa mean complete or whole: el cuento completo, “the complete tale”; la lista completa, “the complete list”. Falta as a feminine noun is an absence or missing item; the inventory label «falta: libro de la biblioteca» records that absence. Faltar is the previously met verb “be missing”. The identical written falta can therefore serve different grammatical roles; do not count every occurrence as evidence for the new noun sense.

The record marked falta remains in Elena’s notebook while the new complete list records the recovered and purchased books. The letter and unreadable signature from chapter11 remain separate from the new request inside the recovered book. That new paper asks ¿Los recogen el domingo?, “Will you collect them on Sunday?”, using a scheduled present question about the six books. It does not establish a donation or identify the earlier letter’s sender. For the final personal question, give your own preference and a reason. Its sample answer is only an example.

items.rubric: For story questions, give the relevant fact in your own complete Spanish sentence. For the final personal question, give your actual preference and a reason; the model is only an example. Other correct wording is welcome.
